arml-1996-team-01.title: Average height
arml-1996-team-01.body:
The water surface is a plane, so the water height along the axis is the average of the highest and lowest heights, $\frac{9+3}2=6$. The volume is the base area times this average height: $V=\pi\cdot2^2\cdot6=24\pi$.

**Answer: $24\pi$**

arml-1996-team-01.title: Two copies make a cylinder
arml-1996-team-01.body:
Imagine a second congruent solid of frozen water and flip it upside down onto the first so that the two tilted surfaces coincide. Together they form a cylinder of diameter $4$ and height $9+3=12$, of volume $\pi\cdot2^2\cdot12=48\pi$. The water is half of it: $24\pi$.

**Answer: $24\pi$**

arml-1996-team-02.title: Choose two vertical segments
arml-1996-team-02.body:
The row has $174$ vertical segments (the two ends of each square, shared between neighbours). A rectangle is determined by choosing any two of them as its left and right sides: $\binom{174}{2}=\frac{174\cdot173}{2}=15051$.

**Answer: 15051**

arml-1996-team-03.title: Q(1) is the derivative
arml-1996-team-03.body:
Let $P(x)=37x^{73}-73x^{37}+36$. Since $P(1)=0$, $P(x)=(x-1)Q(x)$. The sum of the coefficients of $Q$ is $Q(1)=P'(1)$ (differentiate: $P'(x)=Q(x)+(x-1)Q'(x)$). Now $P'(x)=37\cdot73x^{72}-73\cdot37x^{36}$, so $P'(1)=0$.

**Answer: 0**

arml-1996-team-04.title: Find the possible digit multisets
arml-1996-team-04.body:
A digit $d$ appears exactly $d$ times, so the digits used are distinct values $d_1,\dots,d_k$ with $d_1+\dots+d_k=6$ (and $0$ cannot appear). The sets are $\{6\}$, $\{5,1\}$, $\{4,2\}$, $\{3,2,1\}$.

| digits | arrangements | digit sum | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| six 6s | $1$ | $36$ | $36$ |
| five 5s, one 1 | $\frac{6!}{5!}=6$ | $26$ | $156$ |
| four 4s, two 2s | $\frac{6!}{4!2!}=15$ | $20$ | $300$ |
| three 3s, two 2s, one 1 | $\frac{6!}{3!2!1!}=60$ | $14$ | $840$ |

Total: $36+156+300+840=1332$.

**Answer: 1332**

arml-1996-team-05.title: Bound the digits
arml-1996-team-05.body:
$M=\frac{10^{300}+8}{9}$. Suppose $N$ has $n$ digits, so $N<10^n$, and $MN$ has $Kn$ digits, so $10^{Kn-1}\le MN$. Then $9\cdot10^{Kn-1}\le(10^{300}+8)N<(10^{300}+8)10^n$, which gives $Kn-1<300+n$ (roughly), i.e. $K<\frac{301}n+1$. This is largest for $n=1$, where $K\le301$.

$K=301$ is attained with $N=9$: $MN=10^{300}+8$ has $301$ digits, and $N$ has $1$.

**Answer: 301**

arml-1996-team-06.title: Angles in the kite
arml-1996-team-06.body:
Let $\alpha=\angle AOP$. Then $\angle AOB=2\alpha$ and, since $OAPB$ is a kite with right angles at $A$ and $B$, $\angle APB=180^\circ-2\alpha$. So $\tan2\alpha-\tan(180^\circ-2\alpha)=2\tan2\alpha=-\frac83$ and $\tan2\alpha=-\frac43$. With $t=\tan\alpha>0$: $\frac{2t}{1-t^2}=-\frac43$, so $2t^2-3t-2=0$, $(2t+1)(t-2)=0$ and $t=2$.

Take $OA=1$; then $AP=2$ and $OP=\sqrt5$. The ratio of radii is $\sqrt5$, so $x=5$.

**Answer: 5**

arml-1996-team-07.title: Layers of vertices
arml-1996-team-07.body:
The shortest path has length $3$ edges. The $12$ vertices form layers: $A$, its $5$ neighbours $C$, then $5$ vertices $D$ (neighbours of the opposite vertex $B$), then $B$. From $A$ there is $1$ edge to each $C$. Each $C$ is adjacent to exactly $2$ of the $D$ vertices (the ring of $D$'s is a pentagon, and each $C$ sits above an edge of it). Each $D$ is adjacent to $B$. So the number of paths is $5\cdot2\cdot1=10$.

**Answer: 10**

arml-1996-team-08.title: x-intercepts
arml-1996-team-08.body:
The line $y-10=m(x-3)$ has $x$-intercept $3-\frac{10}m$. The base of the triangle is $\left|\frac{10}{m_1}-\frac{10}{m_2}\right|$ and its height is $10$, so $200=\frac12\cdot10\cdot10\left|\frac1{m_1}-\frac1{m_2}\right|$, i.e. $\left|\frac1{m_1}-\frac1{m_2}\right|=4$.

Since $m_1\le0.24<1\le m_2$ (an integer slope is at least $1$), $m_1<m_2$ and $\frac1{m_1}=4+\frac1{m_2}$, so $m_1=\frac{m_2}{4m_2+1}$. The condition $m_1\le0.24=\frac6{25}$ reads $25m_2\le24m_2+6$, i.e. $m_2\le6$. Hence $m_2=1,2,\dots,6$ (all give $m_1>0$), that is $6$ values.

**Answer: 6**

arml-1996-team-09.title: Menelaus twice
arml-1996-team-09.body:
Here $DB=115-38=77=CF$ and $AF=115+77=192$.

Menelaus in $\triangle ABC$ with transversal $D,E,F$: $\frac{AD}{DB}\cdot\frac{BE}{EC}\cdot\frac{CF}{FA}=1$, so $\frac{38}{77}\cdot\frac{BE}{EC}\cdot\frac{77}{192}=1$ and $\frac{BE}{EC}=\frac{192}{38}=\frac{96}{19}$.

Menelaus in $\triangle ADF$ with transversal $B,E,C$: $\frac{AB}{BD}\cdot\frac{DE}{EF}\cdot\frac{FC}{CA}=1$, i.e. $\frac{115}{77}\cdot\frac{DE}{EF}\cdot\frac{77}{115}=1$, so $DE=EF$.

Triangles $CEF$ and $BED$ have equal (vertical) angles at $E$, so $\frac{[CEF]}{[DBE]}=\frac{CE\cdot EF}{BE\cdot ED}=\frac{CE}{BE}=\frac{19}{96}$.

**Answer: $(19,96)$**

arml-1996-team-10.title: Reduce to a sum of floors
arml-1996-team-10.body:
Since $\lfloor n+r\rfloor=n+\lfloor r\rfloor$ for an integer $n$, $N(x)=\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor6x\rfloor+\lfloor15x\rfloor+\lfloor65x\rfloor+\lfloor143x\rfloor$.

Hence $N$ is a non-decreasing step function, and the number of values it takes is $1+{}$(the number of distinct points of $(0,1]$ where it jumps). The jumps occur exactly at the fractions $\frac k6$, $\frac k{15}$, $\frac k{65}$, $\frac k{143}$ in $(0,1]$ (and $\lfloor x\rfloor$ jumps at $1$, which is among them). Count the union $A\cup B\cup C\cup D$ of these four sets, of sizes $6,15,65,143$, by inclusion-exclusion:

- Pairwise intersections: $A\cap B$ is the fractions with denominator dividing $\gcd(6,15)=3$: $3$ points; $B\cap C$ ($\gcd=5$): $5$; $C\cap D$ ($\gcd=13$): $13$; the other three pairs share only $x=1$: $1$ each. Sum: $3+5+13+3=24$.
- Triple intersections: each is $\{1\}$, four of them: $4$. Quadruple: $1$.

Union $=229-24+4-1=208$ jump points, so $N$ takes $208+1=209$ values.

**Answer: 209**
